pitch_detail.notes: Start at the pair of parallel cracks about 150 ft left of the Clean Break start on Juno Tower's east face. Climb the twin cracks, a pleasant moderate opener, to the base of the second pitch's flake.
The crux: an offwidth flake. The route takes gear up to 6 in, and the big pieces are for this pitch; a standard rack alone will leave the wide section poorly protected.

Traverse left through brushy ground rather than going straight up: the blank slabs directly above take no protection, which is why the line veers off. Easy climbing, but manage rope drag through the vegetation.

Easy climbing to a pair of trees used as the bail anchor, where the route ends well below the top of the tower. Descend from here with two double-rope rappels straight down the line of ascent to the base.

review.changed: Same four pitches and labels; notes expanded from one phrase each. P4 lengthM (15.2) DROPPED: the stored note admits it was back-filled from the 350 ft total minus the other pitches, which the brief forbids. P1-P3 lengths rounded (27/24/40 m from 90/80/130 ft). Only P4's anchor (trees) is stated; no other anchors or bolts given, and none added. Single source (Mountain Project, no comments), hence medium. Only thin data exists, so the notes stay short rather than padded.
review.other_findings: None. Stored grade 5.9, 4 pitches, 107 m (350 ft), the FA and the two double-rope rappels all match the source.

pitch_detail.notes: Pull over or around the short wall capped by a 3 in horizontal crack, then follow low humped ridges to two diagonal cracks. Pass a cedar bush on its left to blocks in a right-facing corner. A bolt protects the step left onto knobs and a dirt pedestal. From its top, step down and left across a deep cleft to big cracks and knobs to the anchor.

A clean slab on small edges past a bolt leads to an exfoliation crack. Most of the pitch is a long undercling up a grassy, dirt-filled 1 in crack whose gardened slots take gear well; doubles from 0.75 to 2 in are useful. Near the top, step right on edges over two small overlaps to the anchor.
Keep underclinging along the seams between granite layers, friction for the feet, past one bolt. A second bolt near the top protects the move over an overlap, which goes on good knobs.

Up a shallow groove where protection is hard to find, taking the best rock on the right of a large tree patch. Cross left above the trees, where the rock turns crumbly on the pull onto a broad, lower-angled ledge. Scramble diagonally left to the anchor on the very edge of the buttress crest.
Angle right across a stretch of blank rock to a set of narrow dihedrals, then climb into a slot between two exfoliating sheets of granite.
A jagged finger crack with good gear starts the pitch. It then hugs the right side of a tree patch before easing onto lower-angle knobs and smears.
Unremarkable ground up blocks, tilted ramps and lichen-covered slabs. Stay on the cleanest rock; the overlaps to either side are heavily lichened.
More moderate face climbing, on noticeably cleaner rock than the pitch below.

Head for an S-shaped crack that takes gear but narrows below finger width. A bulge above goes right on smearing moves. Blocks and flakes then lead to the chains on the ridge top, the same anchor that tops pitch 11 of Concerto in C for Drill and Hammer.

From here the route follows the ridge to the summit alongside Concerto in C for Drill and Hammer's pitches 12-14. Keep to good rock on the ridge's right margin rather than thrashing through the brush on top. Climb blocky, ledgy ground up the right side of the crest to a chain anchor on the crest. Bolts are sparse on the ridge.
Scramble up the ridge until trees push you right, then step down onto the slab layer just below them. Follow its dihedral, which protects well, to a chain anchor on a small stance.

Step right past an obvious clean 3 in crack and around the bulge up and right. Climb a rib with a horizontal slot for a small piece, then a bolt, and pass some bushes to a white rib with a second bolt. Keep left of a tree and push through its branches into wide cracks between blocks, reaching the chain anchor on the summit.

review.changed: Same 12 entries, labels and grades for P1-P9; notes rewritten from one clause to the full pitch description. New: bolt counts where stated (P1 1, P2 1, P3 2, P9 2, P12 2). Anchors: 'bolted' for P1-P8 (the 2023 rappel anchors) and 'chains' P9-P12. P10-P12 were 'variable' with no content; they now carry the shared Concerto pitch 12-14 grades (5.5/5.6/5.7) and descriptions. LEFT OUT: bolt counts for P4-P8 and P10-P11 (the source gives none; it may be zero but does not say so), and lengths for P10-P12 (not stated). Crux flag on P9: the route's only 5.9 and called the crux in the stored beta. P1-P9 come from one detailed source, hence medium.
review.other_findings: The Concerto page says its final FOUR pitches were climbed earlier as part of Primal Scream, but the Primal Scream page joins at Concerto's pitch-11 anchor and shares only three pitches (12-14). The stored overview's 'sharing its final three pitches' matches the Primal Scream page. No change suggested.

pitch_detail.notes: Start as for Beckey-Tate on the broken ledge system at the base of the south face. Then break hard right across a series of overlaps to a large ledge at the foot of a clean open-book corner. The traverse is the route's own start: do not continue up Beckey-Tate.
The first of two clean, classic corners, climbing the open book above the ledge.
The second clean corner, which runs through a burly, strenuous bulge, the hardest move on the route.
Continue up slabs, then exit through a wide crack in poor rock, testing holds before weighting them. Belay beneath a large roof.
Avoid the roof on easy cracks to one side and follow them to the top of the wall.

review.changed: Five pitches kept with their labels. All stored parenthetical grades removed. Only P3 keeps a grade (5.11c, the bulge in the second corner). The stored 5.8-5.9 (P1, P5), 5.10 (P2) and 5.10+ (P3) are NOT supported by any source found, so P1, P2, P4 and P5 carry no grade. Every stored lengthM (52/52/52/52/51) DROPPED: they are the 850 ft total split evenly, not measured pitches. The crux moves from stored P4 to P3. The one source lists the sequence as traverse, corner, corner-with-bulge, slabs plus wide crack to a belay under the roof, then easy cracks. Mapping those five stages onto P1-P5 is a reading of that sequence, not a stated pitch-by-pitch breakdown. The stored table had the two corners on P2 and P4 with a 'continued corner' P3 between them, which the source does not describe. Single source (the FA party's AAJ report), hence medium. The reviewer may prefer to SKIP if unnumbered stages are unacceptable.
review.other_findings: The FA report says the finish BYPASSED the big roof via easy cracks to the top of the wall. Stored beta/overview say it exits 'to the summit', and the descent assumes the summit, but the source only says 'top of the wall'. Stored length_m 259 = 850 ft and the grade 5.11c both match. The stored beta's 'wide-crack section followed by easier cracks' omits that the wide crack has poor rock.

pitch_detail.notes: Shared with Let it Burn and the West Face. A few steep moves up the broken ramp system trending right, past a tree, then easier ground to a flat ledge below a vertical splitter. Grades given for this pitch range from 5.7 to 5.8.
A short thin-hands splitter, roughly 25 ft of hard climbing, then easier ground up and left along the ledge to the trees at its far left end for the belay.

Finger cracks lead to a V-slot with a thin crack. The flakes on the left are detached: step on them rather than pull. Go up and right past a small roof, then traverse left past two bolts on the crux moves. Finish on knobs and a finger crack to a two-bolt belay. The old fixed pin is gone and leaves a good cam placement.
Hands and fingers on knobs, fins and thin cracks, stepping right twice into new crack systems, to a double crack. Belay at a fixed pin and a bolt on a small ledge.

Move into the right-slanting flared slot, mantle right onto a square ledge, then make a powerful layback past an overhanging flake. Near the top of this pitch Accendo Lunae leaves Let it Burn: belay on a bench to the right, on gear around 1 in.

New terrain. Traverse right, then climb a gently overhanging line of thin cracks and tips locks. The crux passes a wedged flake that flexes, so gear placements beside it are unreliable. Belay in a small alcove in the chimney just right of a razor-sharp flake. Grades for this pitch range from 5.11c to 5.12-.

New terrain. Awkward body positions up a tips crack in a V-shaped flare lead to a stance under a 4 ft roof where the corner switches from right-facing to left-facing. Good gear overhead protects a double hand-jam pull over the roof into thin hands, which fights up to a ledge. Grades given run from 5.11- to mid-5.11.
Back on the West Face for its crux: a perfect hand crack up the arching corner to an even bigger roof, surmounted on its left side to a stance. Grades range from 5.11c to 5.12-.

The West Face's overhanging chimneys. Fight past the first overhang into a squeeze chimney, exit to a crack, then into a second flaring chimney. Step right at a big block to belay on a large ledge. Originally rated 5.8, it is widely regarded as climbing like 5.10.

Easy blocky ground up and right to the summit, usually simul-climbed. A notch on the far right gives quick access to the walk-off. From the summit block a single 30 m rappel east off a slung horn reaches the descent.

review.changed: Same 10 pitches and labels. All 'lengthM: null' keys removed. P10 gets lengthM 91 from the stated 'easy 300 feet'; no other length is stated. Notes rewritten with pitch-level features. P1 grade 5.8 -> 5.7 (5.7 in three sources, 5.8 in one; the range is stated in the note). Added: P3 bolts 2 and a bolted anchor (the 2025 description reports two anchor bolts where the older one listed one bolt plus gear, and the fixed pin is removed). Also added anchors P1/P2 tree, P4 fixed pin + bolt, P5 gear. LEFT OUT: the crux flag (P3 and P6 are both 5.12- and the FA party later downgraded P6), anchors on P6-P9, and all other lengths. P1-P5 are cross-checked in three sources, P6-P9 in two.
review.other_findings: 1) The stored beta still says P3 passes 'a 5.11 slot with a fixed pin' and belays 'with one bolt and gear'. The pin has since been removed and the anchor now has two bolts. 2) The FA write-up lists P1-P2 as part of the West Face and gives P1 5.7, P4 5.11-, P7 5.11 and P8 5.12-. The stored beta/overview follow the Mountain Project grades, which the reviewer may want to hedge. 3) The stored 'rappels' column says the Let it Burn half can be rappelled with two ropes, which none of the sources consulted state (the FA party walked off).

pitch_detail.notes: The lowest section of the north ridge is easy fourth- to low-fifth-class ground, often climbed tied in but with little or no gear. It ends at slings for a 25 m rappel into the first (lower) notch. Many parties skip it and start at that notch, contouring up from the Sherpa-Argonaut basin and scrambling easy slabs before roping up.

From the lower notch the ridge steepens and offers many options. Keep just left (east) of the crest; straying onto the crest at the wrong point adds harder 5.6-5.9 pitches. The section mixes class 2-4 ground with several 5.7-5.8 pitches and is usually simul-climbed. It ends on top of the large tower about two-thirds of the way up the ridge.

From the big tower walk down, then rappel 25 m from slings (or downclimb) into the second notch. It is also possible to drop about 60 ft and traverse around the tower to a large ledge with bivy space. Cross the narrow knife-edge bridge beyond (class 3-4), scramble around a couple of spires, and pass the big gendarme with the diving-board feature on its right.

The first of two short, steep pitches guarding the summit section. Large detached blocks and awkward protection are common on the pitches above low fifth class, so test holds and place gear with care.
The second short, steep pitch, reached across a stretch of class 2-3. Expect the same mix of solid cracks and loose, detached blocks as the pitch below.
Several blocky steps lead to the summit. Most are low fifth class, but a few are short, bouldery 5.8+ moves. Descent begins from the summit anchor with a short rappel to the southwest.

review.changed: Five stored sections kept with their labels, grades normalised to chips/tokens, notes expanded. One section ADDED at the start ('Toe of the ridge'): the lowest ridge section and its 25 m rappel into the lower notch. One source climbs it; the other says most parties start at that notch. The 25 m rappel lengths come from one source. Lower-section and notch grades changed from sentences to chips. LEFT OUT: lengths, bolts and anchors (none stated), and any crux flag (two 5.8 pitches plus 5.8+ boulder steps; no single crux is identified).
review.other_findings: 1) The stored descent_text says 'parties have reported the full descent taking about 10 hours from the summit'. The source reports about 10 hours on the ROUTE (the climb), not the descent, so that sentence is wrong. 2) Rock quality is contested: one report calls the rock solid and very good, another reports large detached blocks on almost every pitch above low fifth. The stored overview's 'sustained loose rock' states only one side. 3) Area check: the sources file this route on SHERPA PEAK. The catalog area 'Sherpa Balanced Rock' appears to be that peak (it has a balanced summit block); worth confirming the area name is intended.

pitch_detail.notes: Start on the right side of the south face, above the East Nooksack Glacier, and front-point partway up the snow chute. Exit left onto a sloping ledge and change from crampons and boots to rock shoes; carrying the boots and tools up the rock makes for heavy packs.
The first rock pitch, close to a full 60 m rope, angling slightly up and left. The first several pitches pass a short overhanging bulge on the way to a large depression.
The crux: 5.10- moves with a big runout on poor rock. Protection is limited throughout the face, and this pitch is the most serious lead on it.
Easier fourth-class ground up and left into the gully/depression.
Continue left on fourth-class and low-fifth-class rock. At the end of the rope, simul-climb up and left out of the depression toward the buttress on the left-center of the face.
An exposed traverse into the heart of the buttress with moves of perhaps 5.9, on loose rock with very little protection.

Three to five pitches of mid-fifth-class climbing straight up the buttress, in places loose and dirty. Protection is sparse but adequate, and the exposure is severe. The section ends at a short downclimb of about 10 ft.
A strenuous hand crack right after the downclimb. Protection is good and plentiful, but holds break, so it feels harder than its grade.

Two or three pitches of low fifth class to the top. Staying on the buttress leads onto a small tower that needs a rappel of about 50 ft just below the summit, then easy fourth-class rock to the top. Descend by the standard north face route.

review.changed: 3 range rows -> 9 entries. The stored 'Pitches 1-3: steep snow/ice to ~55°' was wrong: the snow is a short couloir climbed partway before the first rock pitch. The stored '4-8'/'9-12' rows were both '5.9-5.10-' with no detail. The old labels name no longer-existing groupings, so all are replaced. The 5.10- crux is placed on rock pitch 2 because the FA account calls it the crux. The snow is 40-50° in the trip report and to 55° in the AAJ note, hence the chip. Lengths only where stated (P3 50 m, P5 40 m). LEFT OUT: grades for P1 and P5. P5's '5.9' is the leader's uncertain estimate, so it stays in the notes as 'perhaps 5.9' rather than the grade field. The upper pitch numbering is also omitted: the FA account gives '3-5' and '2-3' pitches and the total is 12, so numbering beyond P5 would be invented. Both sources are by the FA party (only known ascent), hence medium.
review.other_findings: 1) FA DATE: the stored fa says 'July 2002', but the FA party's own trip report is dated July 23-25, 2001 ('first to summit in 2001'). The AAJ note is in the 2002 publication year and says only 'In July', so the ascent was July 2001. 2) The stored approach puts the face base at ~6,500-7,000 ft, which the sources do not state (6,500 ft is the party's CAMP on the Price/Nooksack shoulder). The approach from that camp is a downclimb and one rappel to a small pocket glacier, a short couloir onto the East Nooksack Glacier, then icefalls; the stored approach omits the rappel. 3) The stored overview's 'poor rock quality and limited protection' matches, but the hand crack near the top is well protected. 4) length_m is null and no source gives a total height.
